events.summary: Jesse Preis debuts The Raven, a chamber opera composed for three voices and chamber ensemble from Edgar Allan Poe’s poem of the same name, directed by Melory Mirashrafi. In this opera, the narrator (split into two characters to capture the perspective of the Past and the Current at two different stages in life) deals with the loss of a loved one. These complicated, painful, and even terrifying emotions become personified through the character of the Raven. This work is composed with no specific voice types tied to the characters - anyone able to sing the part can and should sing them. This is a groundbreaking composing technique that unties the binds of gendered characters and allows vocalists to portray a character of any gender that is authentic to them and suits their voice. Preis seeks to expand our understanding of vocal writing to go beyond the gendered conventions of soprano, mezzo-soprano, tenor, and bass-baritone, and posits a world where characters are simply written and performed by a wide variety of voices.
events.title: The Raven

events.summary: Written in 1936, this light-hearted comedy has relevance for today in addressing the main theme of finding one’s own way in today’s complex society, while lightly viewing such topics as distrust of government, domestic terrorism and fear of foreign conflicts. “Grandpa” Vanderhof (Robert Lovitz) once worked in the competitive business world. One day, he realized he was unhappy, so he stopped working. Since then, he spends his days catching and raising snakes, watching graduation ceremonies, visiting old friends, and doing whatever else he wants. His daughter Penny (Marilyn Stacey) writes plays simply because a few years ago a typewriter was delivered to the house by accident. His son-in-law Paul Sycamore (Todd Hermanson) spends hours in the basement making illegal fireworks and playing with erector sets. His granddaughter Essie (Bonnie Auguston) sells candy and has been clumsily attempting ballet for over eight years. His grandson-in-law Ed Carmichael (Aiden Brown) plays the xylophone (or tries to) and accidentally distributes Marxist propaganda. Joining this free-for-all are Rheba (Caren Graham), the household cook; her unemployed boyfriend, Donald (Shaun Hennessy); Essie’s opinionated Russian ballet instructor, Mr. Kolenkhov (Mark Schwahn); Olga (Trisha Todd), a Russian Grand Duchess; Gay Wellington (Adrienne Southard), a heavy-drinking actress; Wilbur C. Henderson (Douglas Hout), a forlorn IRS employee; and Mr. De Pinna (Danny Bruno), a deliveryman who arrived 8 years ago and decided to stay. He now helps with the fireworks and dresses in Roman togas to pose for Penny’s portraits. All is somewhat calm until three men from the government (Christopher Sparks, Dan Weiss, and Erik James) visit to investigate Ed’s flyers. In this crazy mix of characters, there is also Alice (Taylor Jean Grady), Penny and Paul’s other daughter and, apparently, the only “normal” family member. She met Tony Kirby (Noah Matthew Rich) at his dad’s Wall Street investment firm, and they’ve fallen in love. Culture shock and fireworks fly when Mr. Kirby (Jeremy Southard) and Mrs. Kirby (Wendy Martel) come to visit. But the message is clear: “Life’s pretty simple if you just relax,” as Grandpa puts it. You Can’t Take It With You is directed by Don Alder. Set design is by Chris Whitten, lighting design is by Demetri Pavlatos, costume design is by Janelle Sutton, prop design is by Allen R. Phillips, the stage manager is Alex Salem, the assistant stage manager is Nat Weinham, and the producer is Steve Knox.

events.summary: Adapted from Agatha Christie’s classic mystery, this immersive production brings the psychological tension of the classic tale into immediate, breath-held proximity. Our story takes place inside a remote seaside mansion after a violent storm strands ten guests and their hosts. When an eerie accusation recorded on a gramophone accuses each of them of wrongdoing, the guests confront secrets, guilt, and suspicion. Trapped by weather and circumstance, alliances form and fracture… old grievances surface, and rationality gives way to intense fear as each new death raises the stakes. At ETP’s production, you’ll find yourself sitting with the characters within the house itself, among the bedrooms, the dining room, and narrow passages. Experience the shifting power dynamics and mounting claustrophobia as if you were part of the action. Hear whispered confrontations up close, overhear private confessions, and feel the silence before the next crisis. Though the environment surrounds you, the audience is strictly non-participatory — as a silent witness, a “fly on the wall,” you will never be directly addressed by the characters, nor asked to participate. What to expect in performance: \- Tension-driven mystery with tightly controlled pacing and sudden shocks. \- Strong emphasis on atmosphere: storm sound design, flickering lantern and candlelight, thunder, and selective blackout moments. \- Intense emotional scenes: accusations, breakdowns, moral reckonings, and desperate attempts to find the culprit. \- Minimalist, realistic set dressing that transforms the performance space into a lived-in island mansion, with audience seating integrated into set locations (chairs, benches, window alcoves). \- No audience interaction; observers remain silent and stationary throughout each performance. Content warnings: Multiple onstage deaths and depictions of violence (staged, non-graphic). Mature themes and dialogue — recommended for ages 13+ About Experience Theatre Project: Experience Theatre Project is an innovative, immersive theater company based in Aloha, Oregon. Unlike traditional theaters with rows of seats and a proscenium stage, ETP crafts imaginative and fully surrounding narratives, drawing inspiration from both original and classic stories. Our specialty lies in presenting these tales in an unconventional, unexpected fashion, surrounding audiences in the world of the play, similar to a haunted house or a Disney experience. Limiting audiences to sixty or fewer ensures an intimate and memorable experience. Ticket link: www.experiencetheatreproject.org
events.title: ETP Presents Agatha Christie's And Then There Were None

events.summary: By Thy Grace: 25 Years of Mantra North America & Canada Tour 2026 In 2026, Snatam Kaur brings By Thy Grace: 25 Years of Mantra to audiences across North America and Canada. This is a continuation of a decades long journey of shared chanting, prayer, and healing through sound. These concerts are gatherings where stillness, devotion, and collective voice come together to create an experience of oneness and healing. Each concert begins gently and meditatively, building into moments of deep joy and powerful celebration, and finally, ending with stillness and prayer. Together, we will chant the mantras and songs that have held us through life’s greatest challenges and joys, honoring their capacity to bring us back to ourselves time and time again. The title By Thy Grace reflects the heart of this tour. After twenty-five years of recording and sharing her music, Snatam views this work as something carried by the grace of the mantras themselves, the musicians and collaborators who helped to bring them into the world, and the communities who have welcomed these songs into their lives. What began in humble beginnings as unfamiliar sounds to her audiences, has become a living language of healing, known deeply through personal experience. Accompanied by her band, Ram Dass \(piano, clarinet, vocals\), Bruno Justi \(guitar, flute, vocals\), and Sukhmani \(percussion, vocals\), along with some surprise guests, Snatam will share music spanning her discography, featuring well known classics as well as deeply personal songs from Snatam’s history that have never before been performed live, spanning 25 years of music that has become a soundtrack for healing across generations. Each night becomes a remembrance of inner stillness, shared humanity, and of the healing power that arises when voices join together. This tour is an invitation to gather once again, to chant together, and to celebrate the grace that continues to move through these mantras and through all of us.

events.summary: With the same care he combines sound sources into songs, RJD2 has stitched together an impressive career out of many projects: instrumental albums, international tours, credits for Mos Def, MF DOOM, Phonte, producing the theme for Mad Men, and beyond. The Columbus, OH producer titled his new album Visions Out of Limelight in honor of his comfortable place in the underground and his "self-imposed exile" at work on the tracks. For his latest instrumental LP, the producer found inspiration in sources that can be taken for granted by less-discerning listeners. Thanks to time at home with his son, RJD2 was completely immersed in the TV theme songs of the '70s, '80s, and '90s. "I realized how incredibly composed and skillfully complex many of them were. These songs contained a few core tenets: a great groove, a great chord change, a strong melody, and a concise time frame," he says. "It made me realize how hard it is to make instrumental music with a melody that's as memorable as a lead vocal." The producer was also determined to build tracks around interesting basslines, inspired by classic parts in Dr. Dre's "Deep Cover," KMD's "Black Bastards," and \[Diamond D example\]. It was a deliberate change from the chord-centric compositions in post-millennial hip-hop and funk. It became a "mini-mission" for the producer to make a modern album that puts the bass in the forefront of the songs. Both approaches align on single "Catch The Exit Door," as electric bass percolates up and down the neck under wah-wah guitars and horns straight out of a syndicated cop drama. "Through It All" features crooning from English vocalist Jamie Lidell, pondering his existence over piano stabs and a steady breakbeat. Frequent collaborator Jordan Brown flexes his paranoid android falsetto to fit the loose groove of "Fools at the Haul" with robotic precision. Some songs were recorded with live instrumentation while others were chopped and re-assembled via sampler "like the olden days," RJD2 says. "I still to this day appreciate the radical shift in mindstate inspired by constructing a song with bits of found sound." Good luck figuring out which drums are live or samples. With 15+ years of studio experience, the producer has developed a combination of mic placement, technique, tuning and gain staging to get drum sounds that evoke the same grit and urgency of classic hip-hop breakbeats. "You either run out of great drum samples, or you spend the bulk of your creative time chasing new ones, to varying degrees of success," he says. "The finite nature of great drum samples has pushed me further into honing my drumming game." RJD2 has a wide range of Visions: "Wild For The Night"'s aggro horn loop was inspired by the legendary Bomb Squad, while "What I Do, Man" and "Asphalt Lamentations" were inspired by French touch house of Daft Punk and Ed Banger Records. At proper volume, the full album evokes the thrift-shop psychedelia of Paul's Boutique. And the producer really did bury himself up to his neck in the dirt \[where?\] for the album art. "Album covers have become my opportunity to do something fun in the real world," he says. It's a dual homage to Funkadelic's Maggot Brain and Redman's Dare Iz A Darkside two artists with enduring catalogs of no-bullshit, rock-solid music. RJD2 aspires to create a similar body of work, from his 2002 opus Deadringer to 2020's The Fun Ones on to the future. "I have come to terms with the fact that the most impactful and lasting effort I can put, forth in my limited time on Earth is to leave behind the best music I can, not for the sake of pitching 'me,' but for the sake of the music itself," he says. "The timeless nature of recorded music and its ability to touch an unknown future listener makes it as close to a worthy endeavor as I'll ever attempt." Visions Out of Limelight channels RJD2's many influences into another incredible instrumental album, and it just might be a classic one day too. -Jack Riedy

events.summary: English singer/songwriter Beth Orton’s latest album 'Weather Alive' was one of the most critically acclaimed records of 2022, landing on year-end 'Best of 2022' lists from NPR, Pitchfork, and The New York Times—the latter of which praised Orton for her “modal vocal phrases and marveling \[stories\]." Pitchfork also named the title track a Best New Track, calling it “a slow-burning tour de force,” while The Late Late Show with James Corden invited Orton and her band to perform album highlight "Fractals." Orton self-produced 'Weather Alive’, laying the foundations of the album on an upright piano that she installed in her garden shed at home in London. When the time was right, Orton invited an incredible group of collaborators to join her across the album's eight tracks, including jazz poet Alabaster DePlume, The Smile drummer Tom Skinner, multi-instrumentalist Shahzad Ismaily and Mercury Prize nominated bassist Tom Herbert of The Invisible. The musicians locked naturally into Orton’s sensibilities, expanding the emotive and dream-like world she'd created and conjuring a deeply meditative atmosphere that remains long after the final note has evaporated.
events.title: Beth Orton

As they tapped into their infinite fascination with that strange duality, singer/guitarist John McCauley, guitarist/singer Ian O’Neil, drummer/singer Dennis Ryan, and bassist Christopher Ryan assembled a batch of songs exploring desperation, grief, redemption, and resilience with both cinematic detail and lived-in emotionality. A sharp new turn from one of indie-rock’s most enduringly vital forces, Coin-O-Matic arrives as a complicated love letter to a way of life slowly slipping from the collective memory. The follow-up to Emotional Contracts \(hailed by Uncut as one of 2023’s best albums\), Coin-O-Matic takes its title from a cigarette-vending-machine company that served as the headquarters of Raymond Patriarca—a legendary mobster who ran one of the most ruthless crime families in U.S. history. “If you grew up in Rhode Island years ago, you’d see all these mobsters on the news and then run into them at a restaurant on Federal Hill,” says McCauley, referring to Providence’s version of Little Italy. “They were criminals but also very colorful characters, and I wanted the album to partly reflect a certain nostalgia for that kind of seediness.” \(VIP\) Deer Tick VIP Pre-show Experience One \(1\) General Admission ticket Hear Deer Tick play a few songs not featured in the night’s setlist! events.summary: Jason Ross is one of the true rising stars in dance music. He’s been chosen by Above & Beyond for a collaboration on the club mix of ‘Fly To New York’, collaborated alongside Seven Lions to create their festival anthem "Higher Love", worked on mashups with Kaskade, and most recently headlined the 2017 Anjunabeats North America tour. The young beatsmith’s latest single, titled ‘I Will Be There” feat. Lauren Ray, became Record of the Week on ABGT and quickly was supported by the likes of Cosmic Gate, Gareth Emery, ilan Bluestone, Genix, and many more. Jason’s songs are always larger than life, and “I Will Be There” is no exception. Early 2014 saw Jason’s true beginning when “Burma” was released, landing him squarely on the radar of the Anjunabeats A&R team and Above & Beyond, who played the track in their weekly Group Therapy Radio show \(ABGT\). The next week, listeners of ABGT voted “Burma” to be played again as Record of the Week, and then again for the following week’s show. It would be an understatement to say it’s rare for a non-Anjunabeats track to be played in three consecutive episodes of the radio show. For perspective, it’s happened less than 5 times in nearly 600 total episodes going back to 2004. Jason signed to Anjunabeats soon after. His tracks have proven to be bona fide dance floor gold, blasting through sound systems at Madison Square Garden, the EDC Vegas Main Stage, and countless other venues. Above & Beyond and many others continue to see massive crowds surge with excitement whenever they drop a Jason Ross track. The balance of powerful emotion and electrifying energy created in his productions is proving to be a perfect yin and yang, earning him the “future face of trance” crown by Electric Daisy Carnival creators Insomniac. Since “Burma” he has released a sequence of galvanizing tunes on the label, including “Elements,” “Cairo,” and his collaboration with Wrechiski, “Atlas,” which quickly shot up to the \#1 spot on the Beatport Trance chart. Most recently, “Coaster” and “Monarch” have been heaping up praise, including support from the Anjunabeats core of A&B, Andrew Bayer and ilan Bluestone, along with Seven Lions, Armin van Buuren, Gareth Emery, Andrew Rayel, Andi Durrant, Markus Schulz, Ben Gold, Andy Moor, Cosmic Gate, Super8 & Tab, Dennis Shepherd, Kyau & Albert and many more. Jason’s first vocal single, “Me Tonight” featuring Lauren Ray, shot up the Beatport charts to become his second Beatport Trance \#1. As the lead single off of the ‘Anjunabeats Worldwide 06’ compilation, curated and mixed by Jason himself, “Me Tonight” set the tone for an exhilarating, forward-thinking musical journey of Anjunabeats’ exclusives. The compilation is highlighted by six of Jason’s own originals, remixes and collaborations, including two new tracks alongside labelmate ilan Bluestone and a stellar remix of Seven Lion’s hit “Creation.” The compilation charted in the Top 5 of iTunes Dance Albums in seven major markets, including Australia, India, and the United States. Jason is embarking on his first solo headlining tour in support of the compilation, spanning 14 dates and cities across North America, in addition to supporting Above & Beyond at their ABGT200 celebration in September.

events.summary: Each year, Milagro observes Día de Muertos with the premiere of a new production, altar displays, and community events with the Día de Muertos Festival. Portland’s longest-running Día de Muertos celebration turned 30 in 2025, and we are currently in the planning phase for our 31st annual celebration coming this Fall! Stay tuned for information about our 2026 Día de Muertos Celebration! Día de Muertos \(Day of the Dead\) is a long-honored tradition with roots in indigenous Mexican culture. Día de Muertos is observed annually in Mexican and other Latin American cultures on November 1st & 2nd as a remembrance of those who have passed. Individuals and families who honor this day set up ofrendas \(altars\) with offerings to their departed loved ones. Typical offerings include marigolds, calaveras, photos of the dead, and traditional food like “pan de muerto.” Learn more about Día de los Muertos! events.summary: The Multnomah Arts Center (MAC) presents A Good Universe Next Door – A redacted past, a precarious present, and an uncertain future, a group exhibition curated by Celeste Noche and Melanie Stevens. On view in the Front & Center Galleries from September 18 through October 17, 2026, the exhibition features new work by four regional artists: Amber Capwell, Ebony Frison, Maryanna Hollomon, and Orlando Almanza. An opening reception will be held Saturday, September 19, from 1–3 p.m., and an artist talk will take place Saturday, October 10 at 2 p.m. Stevens and Noche invited the artists to consider how utopia and dystopia manifest in their lives, and how they interpret these experiences. Through sculpture, photography, printmaking, and painting, the artists offer visions of futures shaped by remembrance, resistance, solidarity, creativity, and care. Ebony Frison approaches utopia and dystopia as “conditions that coexist within the same historical moment.” Working with archival research, printmaking, photography, and artist books, Frison examines how Black histories persist despite erasure, describing utopia as “a practice of rememory—an active engagement with ancestral knowledge, community care, and historical reclamation.” Maryanna Hollomon highlights the aftermath of war for children and the global systems that produce displacement. “A utopia cannot be achieved without working in solidarity with those most oppressed,” she writes. Her work asks viewers to consider militarism’s impact and to imagine new forms of resistance and collective care. Amber Capwell creates sculptural works that envision utopian possibilities through Tarot readings for endangered Pacific Northwest flora and fauna. “These sculptures exist as a reminder to care,” they write. Their work incorporates queer and trans identities as part of an ecological futurism that demands “a utopia existing where we are allowed to live and thrive.” Orlando Almanza imagines futures built on safety, connection, and community. “I dream of a place where my people can have picnics next to the river, to rest, to laugh… and the grandmothers can enjoy their old age, sitting in their rocking chairs on their front porch,” he writes. “Sueño con el día que pueda ver a mi familia reunida, en la tierra que nos vio nacer” (I dream that one day my family can be reunited, in the land that birthed us). The Multnomah Arts Center is located at 7688 SW Capitol Hwy, Portland, OR, 97219. It is open Monday – Thursday 9 a.m. to 9:30 p.m., and Friday – Saturday 9 a.m. to 5 p.m. Additional Information: The Multnomah Arts Center is a part of Portland Parks & Recreation. MAC offers programs in a wide range of visual, music, movement, theater, and literary arts at an affordable cost to people of all ages. In addition to this vibrant arts education program, MAC runs a community-based visual arts exhibition program, which includes the MAC Front & Center Galleries. MAC also hosts theatre, music and dance performances, and other special events. events.summary: Project details: Join the Hoyt Arboretum Friends Saturday Crew to help care for the trees and trails at Hoyt Arboretum! A reminder email will be sent out a week prior to the event to confirm details. Register Here Meeting location address: 4000 SW Fairview Blvd. Portland, OR 97221 Map to meeting location Parking and meeting location: Volunteers will meet in the maintenance yard behind the Hoyt Arboretum Visitor Center. There are two pay-to-park lots located near the Visitor Center, along with limited free parking along SW Fairview Blvd. Public transit: The MAX Red and Blue Lines drop off at the Washington Park Station and it's about a 15-minute walk uphill via the Overlook Trail to the meeting location. Plan your trip using the TriMet Trip Planner . Volunteers must be 16 years or older: Volunteers between 16 and 17 are welcome to volunteer without an adult, as long as a youth waiver form has been signed by an adult prior to the event. Contact Rowan for more information about this requirement. Location description and accessibility: Volunteers will be working off of established trails and on uneven surfaces. Two single-stall bathrooms and two water fountains are located at the Visitor Center, which may be up to a 15-minute walk from the work site. Questions? Contact Rowan Moreno at rowan@hoytarboretum.org rowan@hoytarboretum.org or 503-823-5453 Thank you for helping to keep Hoyt Arboretum healthy and beautiful! Here are a few tips to get you ready for your stewardship event. Stewardship Crews happen rain or shine. Please dress for the weather and wear long pants with sturdy, close-toed shoes. events.summary: Mark your calendars! Join us October 2, 3, and 4th, 2026 for the annual Portland Greek Festival! Enjoy authentic Greek food, traditional dance, music, and more with the whole family. When the first Greek immigrants came to the Northwest in the late 1800s to work in fishing, lumber, railroad and other jobs, they established the Holy Trinity Greek Orthodox Church in southeast Portland. After they moved to a larger church on 32nd and NE Glisan in 1952, they needed to find a way to pay off the mortgage. The ladies decided to help by holding a bazaar featuring their handwork, food, pastries, music, and dances from their homeland. This was the beginning of what is now known as the Portland Greek Festival. After seven decades, the Portland Greek Festival has become one of the largest festivals of its kind, sharing our Greek Orthodox faith and rich culture with over 15,000 guests annually. The festival is an iconic event in the Portland Metropolitan area and has been designated as an Oregon Heritage Tradition by the Oregon Heritage Commission. Each year a portion of proceeds from the festival goes toward worthy philanthropic endeavors in the greater Portland community. Learn more at www.portlandgreekfestival.com

events.summary: Curated by Harriet Tubman Center for Expanded Curatorial Practice at MLK School and Lisa Jarrett Drawing from the Museum’s collection, this exhibition is co-curated by Lisa Jarrett, an artist, educator, and curator, and the Harriet Tubman Center for Expanded Curatorial Practice at MLK Elementary— a group of 4th and 5th grade curators from KSMoCA. Working from a conversation with notable curators Dr. Lowery Stokes Sims and Dr. Leslie King Hammond, the exhibition engages PAM’s collection in new dialogues shaped by emerging curatorial voices and multigenerational knowledge. From theme and concept development, through work selection, and installation, this community curators project highlights the collaborative nature of curatorial practice and museum work. Harriet Tubman Center for Expanded Curatorial Practice at MLK School \(HTC\) is a KSMoCA project. Students participate directly in shaping exhibitions, positioning them as contributors to the museum, and engaging them as researchers, writers, planners, and curators. Through workshops and field trips, students collaborate with artists, visiting curators, and mentors from Portland State University’s College of the Arts. They research how exhibitions are developed, how artworks are interpreted, and how institutional decisions shape public understanding. Expanded curatorial practice includes visual art, writing, performance, research, publishing, and social practice. Co-founded by Lisa Jarrett and Harrell Fletcher, the project began in 2018 at Harriet Tubman Middle School and continues in its current iteration at Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. Elementary School.

events.summary: Inspired by Katherine Ace’s 9 Portraits as the foundational starting point for the exhibition, Nine Women Artists will feature the work of the artists shown in Ace’s portrait painting. All mature artists in their careers and with a significant presence in the Northwest, their work reveals a diverse expression of artistic styles from representation to abstraction. There are rich details in the painting. Most notably on the left hangs Henri Fantin-Latour’s A Studio at Les Batignolles, 1870 \(Musée d’Orsay\). In this painting is a formal gathering of male artists. In response to this painting, Katherine asked her subjects to dress in their studio/work clothes as counterpoint, all marked in their characteristic poses. Other Portland women artists are recognized here through their paintings—a small Sally Haley still life hangs in the background, as well as an Amanda Snyder painting behind Phyllis Yes. And to the far right, we have a glimpse of Lucinda Parker’s very large work. Postcards and newspapers scattered on the floor are the exhibition announcements and reviews highlighting the artists’ works. An epic portrait featuring nine women artists of the Northwest, Ace responded to the lack of self-portraits by women artists in history. From left, the artists are: Laura Ross-Paul, Katherine’s self-portrait seated with phone, Mary Josephson, Judy Cooke, Phyllis Yes, Sharon Bronzan, Shu-Ju Wang, Lucinda Parker, and Sherrie Wolf. All are women artists who have made long careers in Portland. As Ace notes about these women, “They have tenacity, have lived through sexist decades, told they couldn’t really be artists—only fit for sleeping with the professor, expected to subvert themselves to male artist machismo.”
events.title: Nine Women Artists

events.summary: Chefas Projects is pleased to present Mercurial, a new solo exhibition by sculptural artist Dan Lam, on view September 18 through October 17, 2026. Bringing together more than twenty new works, the exhibition introduces a heightened metallic sensibility to Lam’s singular sculptural language, with surfaces that suggest chrome, liquid metal, and something less readily identifiable-objects caught somewhere between matter and mutation. Known for sculptures that occupy an uncanny space between the organic and the artificial, Lam approaches form as something fluid, seductive, and alive. In Mercurial, this sensibility takes on a distinctly reflective character. Metallic hues course across the surfaces of the works, emphasizing their bulbous contours, dripping edges, and seemingly unstable forms. Chrome-like finishes catch and distort their surroundings, allowing the sculptures to shift with changes in light, perspective, and proximity. The works appear to ooze, pool, drip, and swell. Their surfaces suggest viscosity while their forms remain resolutely sculptural, creating an intriguing contradiction between solidity and liquidity. They seem less like objects that have been made than organisms in the midst of becoming - alien, tactile, and strangely familiar. This tension is fundamental to Lam’s practice. Her sculptures consistently operate between opposing states: attraction and repulsion, organic and inanimate, soft and hard, seriousness and play. Rather than resolving these contradictions, Lam uses them as points of departure. The resulting forms possess an uncanny immediacy, inviting viewers to move closer even as their unfamiliarity introduces a note of hesitation. In Mercurial, the reflective surfaces intensify this exchange between object and viewer. The sculptures absorb fragments of their environments and return them altered, making the surrounding space part of the work. What initially reads as an autonomous object becomes something more relational-a form that changes depending on where it is encountered and how it is seen. Despite their otherworldly appearance, Lam’s sculptures remain remarkably approachable. Playfulness is central to their charge. The works resist the distance sometimes associated with contemporary sculpture, instead engaging the viewer through color, surface, scale, and a visceral sense of recognition. They are strange without being alienating; experimental without abandoning the pleasures of looking. The title Mercurial evokes both the mutable nature of the works and their affinity with mercury: a substance defined by its fluidity, reflectivity, and ability to transform its appearance in relation to its surroundings. Here, Lam translates those qualities into sculptural form. Her objects appear perpetually in motion, suspended between states, as though their final form has not yet been decided. Across more than twenty new sculptures, Mercurial expands Lam’s investigation of the space between the familiar and the unknown. The works activate the imagination through an intuitive visual language - one based not on representation but on sensation. Their exaggerated forms, seductive surfaces, and ambiguous materiality encourage viewers to project, imagine, and participate. In Lam’s hands, sculpture becomes less a fixed thing than an encounter: part organism, part object, part fantasy. Mercurial embraces that instability, presenting a body of work that is at once polished and unruly, seductive and strange, playful and profound.
events.title: DAN LAM | MERCURIAL

events.summary: Chefas Projects is pleased to present Galvanized, the first solo exhibition at the gallery by Portland artist Bobby Adams. On view September 18 through October 17, the exhibition brings together seven new gradient paintings that extend Adams’s ongoing investigation into color, movement, precision, and reduction. Working with hard edges and meticulously calibrated color transitions, Adams constructs paintings that appear at once exacting and elusive. Color becomes both subject and structure: gradients shift across the surface with a measured sense of movement, while simplified compositions heighten the perceptual effects of scale, saturation, and transition. The paintings inhabit a productive space between the mechanical and the handmade, where precision does not eliminate the presence of the artist but makes it more apparent. Adams’s approach is informed by a background outside of traditional art-making. Before turning to painting in 2017, he worked in product development and ran a clothing line for eight years. That experience with materials, systems, color, and visual identity remains embedded in his practice. His paintings share an affinity with the economy and immediacy of graphic design while resisting its fixedness; seemingly simple arrangements become dynamic through subtle shifts in color and proportion. The title Galvanized gestures toward a central tension within the work: the desire to achieve a polished, controlled image alongside the inevitable irregularities of its making. Adams’s paintings are rigorously constructed, but they are not anonymous. Their surfaces hold the evidence of decisions, adjustments, and the physical act of painting. Running through the exhibition is Adams’s longstanding relationship to NASCAR, a significant influence on his upbringing and visual sensibility. The sport’s saturated palettes, speed, spectacle, and graphic intensity provide an unexpected point of departure for paintings that are otherwise characterized by restraint. In California Poppy, this connection is particularly pronounced. Its color relationships carry the visual charge of racing culture while being distilled through Adams’s pared-down formal language. The result is a body of work in which speed is suggested rather than depicted, and where movement emerges from the most economical means. Adams takes visual cues associated with motion, competition, and spectacle and subjects them to the slower, more deliberate logic of abstraction. Galvanized marks an important step in Adams’s relationship with the gallery, following his inclusion in multiple group exhibitions and establishing a sustained presentation of his practice through a focused body of new work.
events.title: BOBBY ADAMS | GALVANIZED

events.summary: For one unforgettable weekend, Thoughts of a Colored Man comes to Portland’s Brunish Theatre in a powerful theatrical experience about identity, brotherhood, vulnerability, joy, love, and what it means to be seen. Written by Keenan Scott II, Thoughts of a Colored Man brings together seven Black men over the course of a single day in Brooklyn, each embodying a different dimension of the human experience. Through poetry, humor, music, movement, and deeply honest storytelling, their lives intersect as they wrestle with relationships, family, ambition, masculinity, community, loss, hope, and the expectations the world places upon them. At once intimate and electrifying, the play moves beyond stereotypes to reveal something far richer: Black men in the fullness of their humanity. They laugh. They love. They hurt. They dream. They disagree. They heal. And, perhaps most importantly, they allow themselves to be vulnerable with one another. Following its acclaimed Broadway run, this Portland production brings this extraordinary work to the Brunish Theatre with a dynamic cast and a commitment to creating an experience that stays with audiences long after the final bow. Whether you recognize pieces of your own story onstage or are being invited into experiences different from your own, Thoughts of a Colored Man asks all of us to look beyond what we assume about one another and consider what becomes possible when people are given the freedom to be fully seen, fully heard, and fully human. Powerful. Poetic. Funny. Moving. Unapologetically human. This is more than a night at the theatre. It is a conversation, a celebration, and an experience you do not want to miss.
events.title: Thoughts of a Colored Man

events.summary: Jesse Preis debuts The Raven, a chamber opera composed for three voices and chamber ensemble from Edgar Allan Poe’s poem of the same name, directed by Melory Mirashrafi. In this opera, the narrator (split into two characters to capture the perspective of the Past and the Current at two different stages in life) deals with the loss of a loved one. These complicated, painful, and even terrifying emotions become personified through the character of the Raven. This work is composed with no specific voice types tied to the characters - anyone able to sing the part can and should sing them. This is a groundbreaking composing technique that unties the binds of gendered characters and allows vocalists to portray a character of any gender that is authentic to them and suits their voice. Preis seeks to expand our understanding of vocal writing to go beyond the gendered conventions of soprano, mezzo-soprano, tenor, and bass-baritone, and posits a world where characters are simply written and performed by a wide variety of voices.
events.title: The Raven

events.summary: For 30 years, Willamette Riverkeeper has worked to protect, restore, and connect people to the Willamette River. That work has only been possible because of people like you. ﻿Now it's time to celebrate! Join us aboard the iconic Portland Spirit for a memorable evening cruise as we honor three decades of conservation, community, and impact—and look ahead to the next chapter of caring for our river. Your evening includes:﻿﻿ Scenic cruise on the Willamette River Exclusive access to the Columbia Deck and ship bow Delicious appetizers Live music Stories and reflections from 30 years of impact Silent auction A chance to celebrate with the community that made it all possible Cash bar﻿ This is more than an anniversary. It's a celebration of the river we all love and the people who have helped protect it for future generations. While the evening will honor the leaders, volunteers, partners, and supporters who built this organization, it is equally about building the future of Willamette Riverkeeper. We hope you will join us, not only to celebrate where we have been, but to invest in where we are going. ﻿﻿ All ages welcome! A 30th anniversary is traditionally known as the Pearl Anniversary a celebration of wisdom, resilience, and beauty that grows over time. We view this as a fitting symbol for our celebration, though in our case, another "pearl" comes to mind. Hidden beneath the waters of the Willamette lives the Western Pearlshell Mussel, a species whose presence speaks to water quality and river health. Like these remarkable mussels, our greatest work often happens quietly, beneath the surface. For 30 years, supporters like you have helped build a healthier, more resilient Willamette—one restoration project, one paddle trip, one volunteer event, one protected river mile at a time. Western Pearlshell mussels can live more than 100 years. We aim to follow their example. Together, we are cultivating a legacy of river health and community that will endure for generations.

On Saturday, October 3 at 7 p.m., North 45 invites longtime regulars, friends, neighbors, and new faces to raise a glass and throw it back to 2006 with an evening of music, food, drinks, and plenty of nostalgia. The anniversary celebration will feature a DJ spinning music inspired by 2006, along with a special menu bringing back one of North 45’s longtime favorites: mussels and frites in several of the “greatest hits,” variations. For two decades, North 45 has been a gathering place for Northwest Portland. The space recently got a fresh look, but it remains a neighborhood pub where friends meet for a drink, fans gather for the big game, and countless memories are made. From first dates and first kisses to birthdays, reunions, celebrations, and everyday nights with friends, the pub has been part of the neighborhood fabric since opening its doors in 2006. “We wouldn’t be here for 20 years without the people who have walked through our doors,” said Josh Johnston. “This celebration is about thanking our patrons, friends, neighbors, and employees who have been part of the North 45 story.” Guests are invited to come ready to embrace the era, bring their favorite memories, and celebrate two decades of good food, drinks, music, and company. events.summary: Run Time: 78 min. TICKETS $15 Doors 6:30 p.m.; Event 7 p.m. Select Showtime to Purchase Tickets Click here to learn more about accessibility at the Tomorrow Theater. THE EXPERIENCE Festival Picks brings together eleven films from nine countries that show just how many ways dance can tell a story and where dance film is now. What ties these films together isn't a single style or theme; it's the exploration that movement can express something words can't. Each filmmaker has a different voice, and that's what makes watching them together so rewarding. This year's collection travels from Colombia, Norway, South Korea, France, Canada, Switzerland, Czechia, Argentina, and the USA, inviting us into eleven distinct worlds, all connected through the universal language of dance. Please note there are flashing lights/strobe effects during the film Boys a Bug. ON SCREEN: Festival Picks: 10 Years of PDFF Más Glow | Directed by Laura Steiner & Choreography by Arci, Lucy Cobaleda, Valentina Ávila, and Valentina Hadad | 3:37 | Colombia - Acrylic nails, pink everything, and the faint sound of a bolero. Más Glow speaks to preconceived notions of beauty, the rules imposed on the female body, and the power in taking up space. As gestures unravel inside a nail salon and dance shifts toward monstrous movement, four women break the rules of how they should behave. VEKK | Directed by Thea Bay and Simon M. Valentine & Choreography by Thea Bay | 6:10 | Norway - A dance film about miscommunication and living in different realities. CE QI NOUS LIE | Directed by Damien Bourletsis | 4:55 | France - What if, within the breath of one body, the echo of another was already resonating? In a vital surge where every movement becomes a cry, nine dancers unveil their inner struggle across shifting landscapes: sea, cliff, city, dance studio, ancient theatre. Nine singular territories. Each surrenders to raw improvisation - a moment of questioning rooted in their intimate space - where movement becomes the language of urgency: to be, to resist, to exist. Bodies answer, intertwine, and merge in an organic continuity, weaving bridges between their solitary battles. Living echoes of an invisible geometry, uniting bodies beyond forms and boundaries. What if what seemed isolated was already part of a vaster, elusive movement? CYPHER | Directed by Ruby Gleber | 4:20 | Argentina - Trapped in an unknown facility, a breakdancer attempts to escape the Figures that hunt him. As he tries to satisfy them, he is met with indifference and violence. CYPHER is a surreal psychological exploration of performance as compulsion and art as confinement. What Is the Dark For? | Directed by Derrick Belcham and Daisy Jacobson & Choreography by Daisy Jacobson | 12:00 | United States - In a minimalist dreamscape, a woman navigates a complex tug of war with a tuxedoed apparition, drawing ever closer to a fated confrontation and a question of her own identity. where is my god | Directed by Hyun soo Gavriel Yun | 3:50 | South Korea - At some point, the body disappears. No weight. No boundary. In that state, I search for God. God never appears. Even at the height of it only silence returns. Does the God within me love me? Boys a Bug | Directed by Laurie Lynch & Choreography by Fraser Roach | 6:16 | Czechia Inspired by Franz Kafka's The Metamorphosis, Boys a Bug explores through ballet the grotesque transformation of a man into an insect, tracing his struggle with fear and confusion as he gradually loses his sense of self. Conceived as a true dance film, it places narrative and cinematography at its center, using movement to express the character's psychological descent. WAIL | Cinematography, Editing, and Color by Juan Pablo Salazar & Screenplay by Clara Thierry | 7:10 | Switzerland - WAIL is a poetic exploration of grief and release. The film merges music, dance, and imagery to embody the act of lamentation. Through an expressive visual and sonic language, WAIL invites the viewer into a sensory space where sorrow transforms into motion, and silence becomes sound. your love: ‘sitting' beside me | Directed and Choreographed by Ali Kenner Brodsky | 4:49 | United States - your love: ‘sitting' beside me is the second section of a triptych of short dance films capturing the life cycle of love. "Sitting" is a movement story that explores the nuances and awkwardness of a budding relationship. LIMBES | Directed by Karl Cannone | 5:32 | France - An expressionist dance film opening a window into the dreams and nightmares of a young man. Between paralysis and release, shadow and light, it reflects on collective fears and traumas, and the winding paths toward healing. Vestiges | Directed by Marcus Eriksson & Movement Direction by Medhi Walerski | 4:59 | Canada - Featuring eleven Ballet BC company artists, Vestiges introduces original choreography and movement direction by Medhi Walerski in close collaboration with the dancers, brought to life through Marcus Eriksson's striking cinematic vision and original score. Shot in a vast, storied space in the Pacific Northwest, the project explores memory and connection through a series of cinematic chapters. ON STAGE: Kailee McMurran, Tia Palomino, Jess Evans Kailee McMurran / Festival Director Kailee McMurran is an award-winning dance filmmaker, performer, and founder/director of Portland Dance Film Fest. A former principal with Rainbow Dance Theatre, she co-founded SubRosa Dance Collective and has performed with Do Jump! Extremely Physical Theater since 2011. She also runs Selkie Stationery, a stationery and watercolor studio. Tia Palomino / Director of Operations Tia Palomino is a performer, teacher, and co-founder of Portland Dance Film Fest. She has performed and taught with Royal Caribbean Cruise Lines, Do Jump! Extremely Physical Theater, Polaris Dance Theatre, POV Dance, SubRosa Dance Collective, and A-WOL Dance Collective. She runs Trampoline Town, a circus studio in SW Portland, where she teaches aerial arts, trampoline, and acrobatics. Jess Evans / Director of Communication Jess Evans is a dancer, choreographer, somatic healer, and co-founder of Portland Dance Film Fest. She has created and performed work as a principal with Rainbow Dance Theater, SubRosa Dance Collective, push/FOLD, and as a solo artist. She is a Licensed Massage Therapist and Certified Mindfulness Meditation Teacher. The pair will screen new material they’re working on and host a discussion about their various artistic projects. Jesse Moynihan worked as a writer/storyboard artist for the Cartoon Network show Adventure Time from late Season 1 until the end of Season 7. He helped create the characters Lemongrab, Ancient Psychic Tandem War Elephant, Maja the Sky Witch, and Jermaine to name a few. He was heavily involved in the story arcs pertaining to Magic Man, Tiffany, Lemongrab, Betty, Wizard City, Glob, and Finn’s grass arm. In 2014 he co-created the animated short, “Manly” for Cartoon Hangover’s YouTube channel. Currently, Jesse lives in Los Angeles recording music for his collaborative studio project Make A Rising and writing and drawing Forming—an eon-spanning epic work of modern mythology about the trajectory of consciousness on planet Earth, now completed and published by Seattle’s Fantagraphics. Dash Shaw is a cartoonist and animator. His latest title, Like Swimmers from New York Review Comics, is a fast-paced mystery in lush painted color that delves into loss, calamity, and whether we ever really know the people we love. His previous graphic novel Blurry was named a “graphic novel of the year” by The New York Times, The Washington Post, Forbes and others. He’s also the cartoonist of Discipline, New School, Bottomless Belly Button, BodyWorld and others. He’s written and directed two animated features, most recently the 2021 film Cryptozoo, which won the Sundance Next Innovator Award. He currently lives in Richmond, Virginia.

events.summary: Sitar virtuoso Arjun K. Verma returns to Portland for a special evening of sitar and tabla, with thrilling rhythms and beautiful melodies that invite the listener into the world of North Indian Classical music. Originally developed with the intention of bringing about inner peace, harmony, and unity, this music is also highly virtuosic, and Arjun carries on the tradition of his teacher, Maestro Ali Akbar Khan, in bringing these qualities to modern audiences. Indian classical music has its roots in the sacred, ancient traditions of India, and has evolved into a sophisticated and beautiful art music, now performed and enjoyed by people the world over. Traditionally, it has been passed along from teacher to student in an oral tradition. North Indian Classical Music has a large repertoire of hundreds of traditional melodies, known as raagas, with thousands of songs and instrumental pieces composed in each. One unique aspect of this type of music is that, though it is firmly rooted in a rich, ancient musical tradition with many elements, there is also a tremendous space for each performer to improvise and express his own feelings. Such a performance is authentically unique, spontaneously composed on the spot, and never duplicated again! The improvisatory nature of North Indian Classical Music provides a rich, fresh, and lively performance for listeners to experience.
events.title: Arjun K. Verma

events.summary: Jesse Preis debuts The Raven, a chamber opera composed for three voices and chamber ensemble from Edgar Allan Poe’s poem of the same name, directed by Melory Mirashrafi. In this opera, the narrator (split into two characters to capture the perspective of the Past and the Current at two different stages in life) deals with the loss of a loved one. These complicated, painful, and even terrifying emotions become personified through the character of the Raven. This work is composed with no specific voice types tied to the characters - anyone able to sing the part can and should sing them. This is a groundbreaking composing technique that unties the binds of gendered characters and allows vocalists to portray a character of any gender that is authentic to them and suits their voice. Preis seeks to expand our understanding of vocal writing to go beyond the gendered conventions of soprano, mezzo-soprano, tenor, and bass-baritone, and posits a world where characters are simply written and performed by a wide variety of voices.
events.title: The Raven

events.summary: Written in 1936, this light-hearted comedy has relevance for today in addressing the main theme of finding one’s own way in today’s complex society, while lightly viewing such topics as distrust of government, domestic terrorism and fear of foreign conflicts. “Grandpa” Vanderhof (Robert Lovitz) once worked in the competitive business world. One day, he realized he was unhappy, so he stopped working. Since then, he spends his days catching and raising snakes, watching graduation ceremonies, visiting old friends, and doing whatever else he wants. His daughter Penny (Marilyn Stacey) writes plays simply because a few years ago a typewriter was delivered to the house by accident. His son-in-law Paul Sycamore (Todd Hermanson) spends hours in the basement making illegal fireworks and playing with erector sets. His granddaughter Essie (Bonnie Auguston) sells candy and has been clumsily attempting ballet for over eight years. His grandson-in-law Ed Carmichael (Aiden Brown) plays the xylophone (or tries to) and accidentally distributes Marxist propaganda. Joining this free-for-all are Rheba (Caren Graham), the household cook; her unemployed boyfriend, Donald (Shaun Hennessy); Essie’s opinionated Russian ballet instructor, Mr. Kolenkhov (Mark Schwahn); Olga (Trisha Todd), a Russian Grand Duchess; Gay Wellington (Adrienne Southard), a heavy-drinking actress; Wilbur C. Henderson (Douglas Hout), a forlorn IRS employee; and Mr. De Pinna (Danny Bruno), a deliveryman who arrived 8 years ago and decided to stay. He now helps with the fireworks and dresses in Roman togas to pose for Penny’s portraits. All is somewhat calm until three men from the government (Christopher Sparks, Dan Weiss, and Erik James) visit to investigate Ed’s flyers. In this crazy mix of characters, there is also Alice (Taylor Jean Grady), Penny and Paul’s other daughter and, apparently, the only “normal” family member. She met Tony Kirby (Noah Matthew Rich) at his dad’s Wall Street investment firm, and they’ve fallen in love. Culture shock and fireworks fly when Mr. Kirby (Jeremy Southard) and Mrs. Kirby (Wendy Martel) come to visit. But the message is clear: “Life’s pretty simple if you just relax,” as Grandpa puts it. You Can’t Take It With You is directed by Don Alder. Set design is by Chris Whitten, lighting design is by Demetri Pavlatos, costume design is by Janelle Sutton, prop design is by Allen R. Phillips, the stage manager is Alex Salem, the assistant stage manager is Nat Weinham, and the producer is Steve Knox.
events.title: You Can't Take It With You

events.summary: Adapted from Agatha Christie’s classic mystery, this immersive production brings the psychological tension of the classic tale into immediate, breath-held proximity. Our story takes place inside a remote seaside mansion after a violent storm strands ten guests and their hosts. When an eerie accusation recorded on a gramophone accuses each of them of wrongdoing, the guests confront secrets, guilt, and suspicion. Trapped by weather and circumstance, alliances form and fracture… old grievances surface, and rationality gives way to intense fear as each new death raises the stakes. At ETP’s production, you’ll find yourself sitting with the characters within the house itself, among the bedrooms, the dining room, and narrow passages. Experience the shifting power dynamics and mounting claustrophobia as if you were part of the action. Hear whispered confrontations up close, overhear private confessions, and feel the silence before the next crisis. Though the environment surrounds you, the audience is strictly non-participatory — as a silent witness, a “fly on the wall,” you will never be directly addressed by the characters, nor asked to participate. What to expect in performance: \- Tension-driven mystery with tightly controlled pacing and sudden shocks. \- Strong emphasis on atmosphere: storm sound design, flickering lantern and candlelight, thunder, and selective blackout moments. \- Intense emotional scenes: accusations, breakdowns, moral reckonings, and desperate attempts to find the culprit. \- Minimalist, realistic set dressing that transforms the performance space into a lived-in island mansion, with audience seating integrated into set locations (chairs, benches, window alcoves). \- No audience interaction; observers remain silent and stationary throughout each performance. Content warnings: Multiple onstage deaths and depictions of violence (staged, non-graphic). Mature themes and dialogue — recommended for ages 13+ About Experience Theatre Project: Experience Theatre Project is an innovative, immersive theater company based in Aloha, Oregon. Unlike traditional theaters with rows of seats and a proscenium stage, ETP crafts imaginative and fully surrounding narratives, drawing inspiration from both original and classic stories. Our specialty lies in presenting these tales in an unconventional, unexpected fashion, surrounding audiences in the world of the play, similar to a haunted house or a Disney experience. Limiting audiences to sixty or fewer ensures an intimate and memorable experience. Ticket link: www.experiencetheatreproject.org
events.title: ETP Presents Agatha Christie's And Then There Were None

events.summary: TICKETS ️ truewest.info/Hakim26 On Sale Friday, June 12th at 10am PT This Event is All Ages ---------------------------------------- Nick Hakim sits somewhere between an analytical philosopher, mystic poet, and abstract painter. To hear him speak of music is to encounter someone who fully understands its power, who has been moved by its magic and seen its miracles. He’s devoted to music as both an ancient artform and eternal medicine. To hear him play music is to feel these truisms in live time. It’s a spirit that the New York-based songwriter has carried in his music—both as composer and collaborator. From early LPs like 2017’s Green Twins and 2020’s Will This Make Me Good, to his new album, I Can See, Hakim has pursued the truth in every note he’s written, every lyric he’s sung. His truth, though, is more akin to the abstract and intangible than the factual—more Borges than George Washington. It's a cosmic assuredness that manifests throughout I Can See; a belief that the good in the universe is good for a reason. Though these songs are older and they represent an uncertain period in Hakim’s life—when he was finishing up a record deal, forming the world of Cometa, and getting out of an extended relationship—I Can See is defined by its clarity. It’s a sharpness alluded to in the title, like feeling a car rattle as it amplifies potent low end or sitting in a hot tub in zero degree weather. “This record felt very cohesive from the beginning. It felt very precious to me and the tricky thing was figuring out what songs to put on the record,” he explains. He arrived at Sonic Ranch with about 40 demos and began picking out which ideas would make it onto the LP. Some of the songs on the album, like “Real Here Now,” are presented as faithful iterations of those first sketches. It lends the album a tactileness, an emphasis on dynamics that is enhanced by this duality. I Can See is a defining statement from an artist who has yet to put out a record that is anything but. And yet, Nick Hakim’s fourth solo LP is a different experience than his previous efforts. It’s bolder, stronger, more confident. Hakim is more intimately attuned to his vision, and there’s not a note on the album that’s out of place. Nick Hakim might shudder at anyone calling him a healer, but this is certainly music for healing, for taking a breath and facing the world with confidence, lucidity, and joy. “There’s something very gentle and very medicinal about this music. Obviously, we all want our music to be heard by people, but I have a different intention with this record,” he explains, before adding: “The intention is for it to connect with people that need it.”
events.title: Nick Hakim

events.summary: It’s rare for an artist with Luke Alexander’s pedigree to rise within the world of electronic music. As the son of a renowned New York City Hip Hop producer, Luke has been immersed in music and art since birth. Raised on the streets of New York, he developed his identity early, rooted in the four loves that define him: music, art and fashion, travel, and his city. While mastering his craft in New York, Luke forged his sound by blending anthemic songwriting with the rebellious edge of mid-2000s American electronic music. He added his signature grit and creativity, resulting in what’s now unmistakably the Luke Alexander sound. From the moment he entered the scene, Luke made waves with bold releases on top-tier dance labels like Spinnin’ Records, Revealed Records, Loudkult, Mixmash, and Oneseven. His work quickly earned the support of industry legends, including Tiësto, Zedd, Diplo, Bingo Players, Laidback Luke, and Loud Luxury. Luke’s energy isn’t confined to the studio—he’s one of the most electrifying live acts in the U.S., performing over 100 shows annually at some of the country’s premier venues, such as Marquee NY, LIV Miami, DAER South Florida, The Brooklyn Mirage, and HQ Atlantic City. From coast to coast, his performances captivate audiences, turning every show into a high-energy spectacle. In 2024, Luke took his talents overseas, dominating international stages with headline performances in Spain, Italy, Ireland, and The Netherlands. He continues to break boundaries in electronic music, bringing people together through his powerful sound and unapologetic vision. A true New Yorker at heart, Luke Alexander embodies the hustle, grit, and perseverance it takes to shape destiny. He’s not just an artist; he’s a force redefining electronic dance music. The New King of New York has arrived.
events.title: Luke Alexander

events.summary: Curated by Harriet Tubman Center for Expanded Curatorial Practice at MLK School and Lisa Jarrett Drawing from the Museum’s collection, this exhibition is co-curated by Lisa Jarrett, an artist, educator, and curator, and the Harriet Tubman Center for Expanded Curatorial Practice at MLK Elementary— a group of 4th and 5th grade curators from KSMoCA. Working from a conversation with notable curators Dr. Lowery Stokes Sims and Dr. Leslie King Hammond, the exhibition engages PAM’s collection in new dialogues shaped by emerging curatorial voices and multigenerational knowledge. From theme and concept development, through work selection, and installation, this community curators project highlights the collaborative nature of curatorial practice and museum work. Harriet Tubman Center for Expanded Curatorial Practice at MLK School \(HTC\) is a KSMoCA project. Students participate directly in shaping exhibitions, positioning them as contributors to the museum, and engaging them as researchers, writers, planners, and curators. Through workshops and field trips, students collaborate with artists, visiting curators, and mentors from Portland State University’s College of the Arts. They research how exhibitions are developed, how artworks are interpreted, and how institutional decisions shape public understanding. Expanded curatorial practice includes visual art, writing, performance, research, publishing, and social practice. Co-founded by Lisa Jarrett and Harrell Fletcher, the project began in 2018 at Harriet Tubman Middle School and continues in its current iteration at Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. Elementary School.
events.title: Harriet Tubman Center Museum

events.summary: Inspired by Katherine Ace’s 9 Portraits as the foundational starting point for the exhibition, Nine Women Artists will feature the work of the artists shown in Ace’s portrait painting. All mature artists in their careers and with a significant presence in the Northwest, their work reveals a diverse expression of artistic styles from representation to abstraction. There are rich details in the painting. Most notably on the left hangs Henri Fantin-Latour’s A Studio at Les Batignolles, 1870 \(Musée d’Orsay\). In this painting is a formal gathering of male artists. In response to this painting, Katherine asked her subjects to dress in their studio/work clothes as counterpoint, all marked in their characteristic poses. Other Portland women artists are recognized here through their paintings—a small Sally Haley still life hangs in the background, as well as an Amanda Snyder painting behind Phyllis Yes. And to the far right, we have a glimpse of Lucinda Parker’s very large work. Postcards and newspapers scattered on the floor are the exhibition announcements and reviews highlighting the artists’ works. An epic portrait featuring nine women artists of the Northwest, Ace responded to the lack of self-portraits by women artists in history. From left, the artists are: Laura Ross-Paul, Katherine’s self-portrait seated with phone, Mary Josephson, Judy Cooke, Phyllis Yes, Sharon Bronzan, Shu-Ju Wang, Lucinda Parker, and Sherrie Wolf. All are women artists who have made long careers in Portland. As Ace notes about these women, “They have tenacity, have lived through sexist decades, told they couldn’t really be artists—only fit for sleeping with the professor, expected to subvert themselves to male artist machismo.”
events.title: Nine Women Artists

events.summary: Get moving with a beginner Tai Chi class by Many Roads Martial Arts Center on Sundays. 10:30 – 11:30 AM | Sundays, May 3 – October 25, 2026 Many Roads Martial Arts Center is offering an introductory Tai Chi class at Lan Su on Sundays at 10:30AM. This class will introduce the fundamental principles of Tai Chi Chaun \(or Taijiquan\) using the Yang Style 24 Posture Form. We will work on posture and body alignment alongside principles of movement and meditation. We will also discuss how Tai Chi blends health, meditation, and martial application. This class is suitable for all levels but will be particularly helpful for beginners of all ages. Get Admission Meet the Instructors: Many Roads Martial Arts Center Jenny Lohr, Owner/Instructor Jenny has been practicing Shaolin Kung Fu and Tai Chi since 2005. As the owner of Many Roads Martial Arts Center, her focus is nurturing a supportive and safe learning environment while challenging everyone to keep growing and improving. Jenny loves the physical and mental challenges of martial arts and is very excited to share them with the students and instructors at the center. Jay Twitchell, Instructor Jay has studied various martial arts systems including boxing, wrestling, judo, karate, taekwondo, aikido, hopkido, kumdo, and muay thai kick boxing since he was 10. In other words, he has been used as a punching bag for over 30 years by masters and lifelong practitioners of these systems. His lifetime of experience getting kicked, punched, choked, kneed, elbowed, and thrown are invaluable in teaching others how not to be. Balancing his martial studies, Jay has 20 years of experience as a massage therapist and movement specialist, offering him a deep knowledge of the human body and healthy practice. Myk Olsen, Instructor Myk has been a Tai Chi Chuan practitioner since 1997 and has been teaching since 2013. His primary teachers were Gao Jamin and Yu Shaowen. Over the years, Myk has learned a multitude of forms in Yang, Chen, Wu, and Sun styles—both open-hand and weapons \(straight sword, broadsword, staff, spear, cane, deerhorn knives, and daggers\). While he used to compete in both forms and Push-Hands, Myk now focuses more time on teaching. His teaching style is student-centered and is focused on achieving a balance between the meditative and martial aspects of the forms. Myk also teaches a Tai Chi class specifically geared toward those with mobility and balance issues on Sunday afternoon. events.summary: Mark your calendars! Join us October 2, 3, and 4th, 2026 for the annual Portland Greek Festival! Enjoy authentic Greek food, traditional dance, music, and more with the whole family. When the first Greek immigrants came to the Northwest in the late 1800s to work in fishing, lumber, railroad and other jobs, they established the Holy Trinity Greek Orthodox Church in southeast Portland. After they moved to a larger church on 32nd and NE Glisan in 1952, they needed to find a way to pay off the mortgage. The ladies decided to help by holding a bazaar featuring their handwork, food, pastries, music, and dances from their homeland. This was the beginning of what is now known as the Portland Greek Festival. After seven decades, the Portland Greek Festival has become one of the largest festivals of its kind, sharing our Greek Orthodox faith and rich culture with over 15,000 guests annually. The festival is an iconic event in the Portland Metropolitan area and has been designated as an Oregon Heritage Tradition by the Oregon Heritage Commission. Each year a portion of proceeds from the festival goes toward worthy philanthropic endeavors in the greater Portland community. Learn more at www.portlandgreekfestival.com
events.title: Portland Greek Festival

events.summary: When we talk about the Declaration of Independence,, we often think of it as a severing from a distant power and a proclamation of individual rights. events.summary: During WWII, young Japanese Americans \(Nisei\) incarcerated at the Minidoka Relocation Center in Southeast Idaho faced a paradox: fight for a country that had stripped them of their civil liberties, taken away their freedom and placed them and their families behind barbed wire, not because they were the enemy but because they looked like the enemy; or, resist the draft because they and their families had been unconstitutionally and unfairly incarcerated. The Nisei Paradox, a theatrical, multi-media stage reading, tells the story of the young Japanese Americans who chose to resist the draft, fighting injustice with civil disobedience from the confines of Minidoka. 32 of them were prosecuted by the federal government; all but one was found guilty. The stage production was created out of the transcripts of these trials in a collaboration between Chief U.S. Magistrate Judge Ronald E. Bush and attorney Jeff Thomson; all the performers are drawn from the legal community. These young men chose a different type of courage than the many Nisei incarcerees who went to war—they chose to resist, to oppose unfair treatment, to stand up to a stacked legal system, only to lose their freedom for a period longer than the 2-year conscription period, longer than the incarceration camps were open, and longer than the war itself. This program is presented by the Japanese American Museum of Oregon and the Oregon Law Foundation.
events.title: The Nisei Paradox: Japanese American Draft Resisters During World War II

events.summary: Written in 1936, this light-hearted comedy has relevance for today in addressing the main theme of finding one’s own way in today’s complex society, while lightly viewing such topics as distrust of government, domestic terrorism and fear of foreign conflicts. “Grandpa” Vanderhof (Robert Lovitz) once worked in the competitive business world. One day, he realized he was unhappy, so he stopped working. Since then, he spends his days catching and raising snakes, watching graduation ceremonies, visiting old friends, and doing whatever else he wants. His daughter Penny (Marilyn Stacey) writes plays simply because a few years ago a typewriter was delivered to the house by accident. His son-in-law Paul Sycamore (Todd Hermanson) spends hours in the basement making illegal fireworks and playing with erector sets. His granddaughter Essie (Bonnie Auguston) sells candy and has been clumsily attempting ballet for over eight years. His grandson-in-law Ed Carmichael (Aiden Brown) plays the xylophone (or tries to) and accidentally distributes Marxist propaganda. Joining this free-for-all are Rheba (Caren Graham), the household cook; her unemployed boyfriend, Donald (Shaun Hennessy); Essie’s opinionated Russian ballet instructor, Mr. Kolenkhov (Mark Schwahn); Olga (Trisha Todd), a Russian Grand Duchess; Gay Wellington (Adrienne Southard), a heavy-drinking actress; Wilbur C. Henderson (Douglas Hout), a forlorn IRS employee; and Mr. De Pinna (Danny Bruno), a deliveryman who arrived 8 years ago and decided to stay. He now helps with the fireworks and dresses in Roman togas to pose for Penny’s portraits. All is somewhat calm until three men from the government (Christopher Sparks, Dan Weiss, and Erik James) visit to investigate Ed’s flyers. In this crazy mix of characters, there is also Alice (Taylor Jean Grady), Penny and Paul’s other daughter and, apparently, the only “normal” family member. She met Tony Kirby (Noah Matthew Rich) at his dad’s Wall Street investment firm, and they’ve fallen in love. Culture shock and fireworks fly when Mr. Kirby (Jeremy Southard) and Mrs. Kirby (Wendy Martel) come to visit. But the message is clear: “Life’s pretty simple if you just relax,” as Grandpa puts it. You Can’t Take It With You is directed by Don Alder. Set design is by Chris Whitten, lighting design is by Demetri Pavlatos, costume design is by Janelle Sutton, prop design is by Allen R. Phillips, the stage manager is Alex Salem, the assistant stage manager is Nat Weinham, and the producer is Steve Knox.
events.title: You Can't Take It With You

THE EXPERIENCE We're all aging. Along the way, we encounter ourselves anew and inhabit the vulnerabilities and freedoms of change. Over the past ten years, we've had the privilege of watching so many filmmakers and dancers in our community grow and evolve, including local artists Suzanne Chi, Carla Mann, and Robert Uehlin. As we reflect on a decade of PDFF, it felt especially meaningful to share their documentary, Still Moving: Dancing Across A Lifetime. The film invites us to think about what it means to keep moving, creating, and dancing as our bodies and lives change. When Suzanne Chi turned 40 during the pandemic, she was forced to confront the question all professional dancers eventually face: should I be done dancing? This feature documentary follows Suzanne and her castmates-five dancers aged 42-65- s they rehearse and perform a new evening-length choreography. In navigating the challenges of aging in an industry that valorizes youth, these dancers offer their own perspectives on how and why they are still moving. Following the film there will be a panel discussion. ON SCREEN: Still Moving Still Moving | Directed by Suzanne Chi, Carla Mann, & Robert Uelin | 39:27 | - This documentary follows Suzanne and her castmates-five dancers aged 42-65 - as they rehearse and perform a new evening-length choreography. In navigating the challenges of aging in an industry that valorizes youth, these dancers offer their own perspectives on how and why they are still moving. ON STAGE: Suzanne Chi, Professor Carla Mann, Rober Uehlin Suzanne Chi is a dancer, producer and curator living in Portland, OR. Performing has taken her around the United States, and to Bulgaria and Germany. She has had the pleasure of working with many Portland based artists and choreographers, and co-directs Muddy Feet Dance with Rachel Slater. Together, Muddy Feet's award winning dance films have been screened all across the world. Professor Carla Mann has been a member of the dance faculty since 1995, teaching beginning through advanced levels of contemporary technique, choreography, improvisation, dance cultural studies and special projects. Her choreographic work includes dance for stage, alternative sites, installation and video. Mann has performed with Oslund\+Co/Dance, tEEth, Bonnie Merrill and Minh Tran & Company among others. Mann was awarded a 2015 Oregon Arts Commission Fellowship and was recently profiled in Stance on Dance. During her 2015-16 sabbatical, Mann will serve as Associate Artistic Director of Heidi Duckler Dance Theatre/Northwest and undertake a new choreographic commission for the Northwest Dance Project. Robert Uehlin is a filmmaker based in Portland, Oregon specializing in the translation of contemporary choreography into the language of film. His work has been screened at the American Dance Festival, The Utah International Screendance Festival, The Sans Souci Festival of Dance Cinema, and across the United States. In 2018, he was selected to receive the inaugural Oregon Dance Film Commission and, the following year, he was named the Hinge Alumni Artist in Residence in West-Central, Minnesota. He has adjudicated for the Portland Dance Film Festival and he is the resident curator of the annual DanceBARN Screendance Festival. events.summary: Jesse Preis debuts The Raven, a chamber opera composed for three voices and chamber ensemble from Edgar Allan Poe’s poem of the same name, directed by Melory Mirashrafi. In this opera, the narrator (split into two characters to capture the perspective of the Past and the Current at two different stages in life) deals with the loss of a loved one. These complicated, painful, and even terrifying emotions become personified through the character of the Raven. This work is composed with no specific voice types tied to the characters - anyone able to sing the part can and should sing them. This is a groundbreaking composing technique that unties the binds of gendered characters and allows vocalists to portray a character of any gender that is authentic to them and suits their voice. Preis seeks to expand our understanding of vocal writing to go beyond the gendered conventions of soprano, mezzo-soprano, tenor, and bass-baritone, and posits a world where characters are simply written and performed by a wide variety of voices.

THE EXPERIENCE We've watched a lot of dance films. For this tenth anniversary, we wanted to revisit a few of the films that have stayed with us. Directors' Picks: A Decade of PDFF is a cohort of nine films from the festival's history that have remained especially meaningful to us. They come from nine countries and span a remarkable range of voices, styles, and stories. Together, these films offer a glimpse into the array of work that has excited and moved us over the years. Please note there is brief nudity throughout this whole program. ON SCREEN: Directors' Picks: 10 Years of PDFF Old Man at the Corner Store, 2023 | Directed by Nadav Heyman and Anabella Casanova & Choreography by Nadav Heyman and Cheryl Mann | 8:10 | United States - An elderly man crosses paths with young neighborhood mischief-makers and dances them through a game of "follow the leader." As they race through the streets, movement becomes their language for exchanging taunts, challenges, and new ways of seeing the world. What I Know So Far, 2022 | Directed by Shawn Fitzgerald Ahern & Choreography by Emilie Leriche | 4:59 | France - A movement-and-words soliloquy that keeps track of small thoughts and fragments of knowledge, shaped as a poetic reminder. Table for one, please., 2024 | Directed and Choreographed by Samantha Shay | 14:10 | Germany & United Kingdom - Emerging from rehearsals for the dance-theater work Life in this House is Over, this short explores the social awkwardness of grief through text, movement, memory, and dramatic vignettes. Inspired by Anton Chekhov, artists connected to Tanztheater Wuppertal Pina Bausch and Teatr ZAR reflect on the blurred boundary between past and future. Dive, 2021 | Directed by Oscar Sansom & Choreography by Sophie Laplane | 13:00 | United Kingdom - Inspired by the visionary work of French artist Yves Klein, Dive immerses Scottish Ballet dancers in a monochrome blue world of empty white space. From stillness, the choreography moves into unexpected complexity, pairing Laplane's distinctive movement with striking, teal-toned cinematography. Second Seed, 2020 | Directed and Choreographed by Amadi "Baye" Washington and Sam "Asa" Pratt | 15:24 | United States - A dance-horror film responding to D. W. Griffith's The Birth of a Nation, Second Seed confronts the white-supremacist mythology and white victimhood embedded in Griffith's film, reframing that history through contemporary Black movement and imagery.
